item.title: Claim-check: The Trump administration has brought $20 trillion in foreign investment into the U.S.
item.description: The $20 trillion figure is President Trump's own claim, which has grown from $17 trillion in late 2025 to $19.2 trillion and then "over $20 trillion" in 2026, but it isn't supported by the administration's own numbers or by government investment data. The White House's own list of "major investment announcements" showed $9.6 trillion in December 2025 and $10.6 trillion in July 2026, roughly half of what Trump cites, and even that list counts multi-year pledges, purchase deals and trade targets (for example, a goal of $1.2 trillion in U.S.-Qatar "economic exchange") rather than money actually invested; Bloomberg Economics estimated about $7 trillion of the $9.6 trillion counted as real investment pledges. Pledges are not investment that has arrived: Commerce Department data showed roughly $145 billion in new foreign direct investment in the first half of 2025, about the same as the year before. PolitiFact rated Trump's $18-22 trillion version False, and CNN's fact-checker called the $19.2 trillion figure "fiction.".

item.title: Claim-check: Tariff revenue helps fund government services, with a fixed share set aside by law for USDA food programs such as school meals
item.description: Tariffs (customs duties) are federal revenue, $194.9 billion in fiscal 2025 (3.7% of all federal revenue) and $173.2 billion in fiscal 2026, and they help pay for government like any other revenue. One slice is tied to specific services by a 1935 law: USDA's Section 32 account receives an amount equal to 30% of the prior calendar year's customs receipts, and most of it is transferred to child nutrition programs such as school meals (an estimated $23.0 billion of $25.2 billion in FY2026, with nearly $82 billion projected for FY2027 from 2025's tariffs). The rest is not earmarked for any program and Congress controls how it is spent; the House Agriculture Committee chair said routing tariff money straight to farm aid didn't appear to be legally possible. After the Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs in February 2026, Treasury reported $125 billion in refunds through August 31, 2026, which the Congressional Research Service says may reduce the Section 32 transfer.

item.title: Claim-check: Rep. Ilhan Omar's birth name is Ilhan Nur Said Elmi
item.description: The name comes from the federal immigration probe of Rep. Omar: a Justice Department motion filed in October 2026 in the fight over unsealing the warrant for the search of her Washington home calls her "Congresswoman Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar" and, Al Jazeera notes, does not explain the relationship between the names. The filing does not say it is her birth name; that rests on two unnamed people familiar with the investigation, including a law enforcement source, quoted by Fox News Digital, and on D.C. U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro, whose office filed the motion and whom Fox describes as confirming on its October 22 Jesse Watters Primetime that it is Omar's "real name" (a segment the government's October 27 court filing cites). Omar's office calls the report "completely false," saying Ilhan Omar is her real name. Elmi is the surname of her former husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, and the dispute has revived the claim that he is her brother, which Snopes found is not supported by enough evidence. No court has ruled on her identity and she has not been charged.

item.title: Claim-check: Climate change isn't real
item.description: Climate change is real and is documented by the federal government's own scientists: NOAA's global record, which goes back to 1850, ranks 2025 as the third-warmest year at 1.17°C (2.11°F) above the 20th-century average, and "the 10 warmest years in the historical record have all occurred since 2015." In September 2025 the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine found that the science behind EPA's 2009 Endangerment Finding is "reinforced by even stronger evidence collected since 2009." The administration has cast doubt on that science (a Department of Energy report by five longtime skeptics, which a judge ruled was produced by a panel that broke federal transparency law, and the dismissal of the National Climate Assessment's authors), but when EPA rescinded the Endangerment Finding it rested the decision on statutory interpretation and the major questions doctrine, not on a finding that climate change isn't happening. TAP documents those government actions in the linked entries at the top of this card.
